etymology: From the prophecy of Isaiah 61:2, “to proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD,” quoted by Christ at Nazareth (Luke 4:19); rooted in the law of jubilee (Leviticus 25), the year of release.
biblical_def: The acceptable year of the LORD is the gospel jubilee—the appointed season of divine favor, of release for captives and recovery for the broken, fulfilled in the person and ministry of Jesus Christ. When the Lord stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth and read from the scroll of Isaiah, He closed the book at “the acceptable year of the LORD,” stopping short of “the day of vengeance of our God,” and declared, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.” In that pause hangs the whole sweetness of the gospel: this present age is not the day of wrath but the day of salvation, the open season of mercy in which the free offer of the gospel goes forth to sinners. As in the year of jubilee debts were forgiven and bondmen set at liberty, so in Christ the soul's vast debt is cancelled and the slave of sin is loosed. This favorable year is not a fleeting twelvemonth but the entire span of grace between Christ's first and second comings—a long, patient day in which the King bids the weary come. Let no man presume upon its length, for the day of vengeance follows close behind; yet while it lasts, the trumpet of jubilee still sounds, and the LORD is well pleased to receive all who come to Him through His Son.
webster_summary: The favorable season of God's grace, the gospel jubilee proclaimed and fulfilled by Christ in His earthly ministry.
webster_full: ACCEPTABLE YEAR OF THE LORD, phrase (biblical expression). From Isaiah 61:2 and Luke 4:19; the year of release modeled on the jubilee of Leviticus 25.
The appointed season in which God is pleased to receive sinners and to dispense salvation freely through Christ.
An allusion to the year of jubilee, wherein debts were remitted and captives liberated, here applied spiritually to redemption in Christ.

As recorded in Scripture: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives… to preach the acceptable year of the Lord” (Luke 4:18-19).
Contrasted with the day of vengeance, the acceptable year denotes the present age of mercy and the open invitation of the gospel.
scriptures: Isa 61:2
To proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;
Luke 4:19
To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
Isa 49:8

Thus saith the LORD, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though its urgency is dulled when grace is treated as endlessly available apart from repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase belongs to the prophetic vocabulary of jubilee and is seldom seized upon for ideological mischief. The danger is rather one of neglect: men hear that this is the year of God's favor and conclude that mercy will always be on offer, presuming upon the patience that should lead them to repentance.

The principle to recover is the urgency of the accepted time. The acceptable year is set against the day of vengeance, and the Apostle presses it home: “now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” The free offer of the gospel is wide and warm, but it is not eternal in its open door. To hear the trumpet of jubilee and delay is to gamble with the soul; the LORD bids us come today, while it is called today.
roots_summary: The phrase grows from the Levitical jubilee, ripens in Isaiah's prophecy, and bears fruit in Christ's Nazareth sermon.
roots_lines: Leviticus 25 sets the pattern: the fiftieth year proclaims liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.
Isaiah 61:2 gathers the jubilee into a Messianic promise of comfort and release.
Luke 4:18-19 records Christ reading the text and applying it to Himself in the synagogue.
The Lord stops at “the acceptable year,” reserving “the day of vengeance” for His return.
Second Corinthians 6:2 presses the present age as the day of salvation now open to all.
usage: Preachers invoke the acceptable year to press the free offer of the gospel upon sinners while mercy stands open.
Believers rest in the truth that this present age is the appointed season of God's favor in Christ.
The phrase warns against presumption, for the acceptable year gives way at last to the day of vengeance.

etymology: From Hebrews 12:2, “Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith”; the Greek archēgos (author, leader, captain) and teleiōtēs (finisher, perfecter) joined as a title of Christ.
biblical_def: Christ is the author and finisher of our faith—the one who begins the work of grace in the soul and infallibly carries it through to glory. The word rendered “author” bears the sense of captain, leader, and originator; the word “finisher” means perfecter, the one who brings to its appointed end. Together they declare that faith is no self-generated work but a gift begun by Christ and completed by Christ. He is the first cause and the last; He lays the foundation and sets the topstone with shoutings of grace. This is the marrow of the believer's assurance and the ground of the saints' perseverance: the same hand that opened blind eyes will not let go of the soul it has seized. As the Apostle reasons elsewhere, “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.” The exhortation of Hebrews is therefore to run the race with patience, “looking unto Jesus”—not unto our own faltering strength but unto Him who for the joy set before Him endured the cross and is now seated at the right hand of God. Because the race He runs in us He also finishes, the weakest believer may be bold; the One who authored faith will most surely finish it, and not one of His own shall perish.
webster_summary: A title of Christ as the originator and perfecter of saving faith, who begins and completes the work of grace in His people.
webster_full: AUTHOR AND FINISHER, phrase (biblical title of Christ). From Hebrews 12:2; Greek archēgos (captain, originator) and teleiōtēs (perfecter).
He that first works faith in the heart and afterward carries it on to its consummation in glory.
The captain or leader who runs before His people in the way of faith and brings them safely home.

As recorded in Scripture: “Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2).
By extension, the sure foundation of the believer's assurance and the ground of the saints' perseverance.
scriptures: Heb 12:2
Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
Phi 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
Heb 2:10
For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
Joh 6:39
And this is the Father's will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the truth is obscured wherever faith is reduced to a human work and salvation made to hang on man's persistence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The title is too plainly Christ-exalting to be openly contested; the error that besets it is the older Pelagian and Arminian tendency to make man the author of his own faith and the keeper of his own soul. Where faith is treated as a self-sprung act and perseverance as a thing the believer must secure by his own grip, the comfort of the text is dissolved.

The principle to recover is monergism in beginning and end. Christ is the captain who runs first and the perfecter who finishes; He does not merely offer faith and leave its completion to us. The 1689 Confession teaches that those whom God has accepted in His Beloved can never finally fall away but shall be kept by His power through faith unto salvation. The weakest saint may therefore look away from himself and unto Jesus, certain that the One who began the work will finish it.
roots_summary: The title gathers the Greek images of captain and perfecter into one confession of Christ's sovereign work in faith.
roots_lines: Archēgos denotes a captain, founder, or originator who leads the way for others to follow.
Teleiōtēs denotes a finisher or perfecter who brings a thing to its appointed completion.
Hebrews 12:2 joins the two as the ground for running the Christian race with patience.
Philippians 1:6 echoes the same assurance: God will perform the work He has begun.
Hebrews 2:10 names Christ the captain of salvation, made perfect through sufferings.
usage: The phrase anchors the doctrine of perseverance: Christ both begins and completes saving faith.
Believers fix their eyes on Jesus as author and finisher rather than on their own wavering strength.
Pastors press the title to comfort fearful saints who doubt they can hold out to the end.

etymology: From the words of Christ in Matthew 11:28, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest”; a personal summons issued by the Lord Himself.
biblical_def: “Come unto me” is the sweetest of all gospel invitations, the very voice of Christ calling the weary and burdened to Himself for rest. The call is wide—“all ye that labour and are heavy laden”—embracing every soul crushed under the weight of sin, of the law's demands, of guilt and care. It is not the strong and self-sufficient who are summoned but the spent and broken, those who have toiled to save themselves and found no rest. To such Christ promises rest, not as a wage to be earned but as a gift to be received: “I will give you rest.” The invitation continues with the gentle yoke: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.” The yoke of Christ is not the galling burden of legal bondage but the easy fellowship of discipleship under a meek and lowly Master. Here is the free offer of the gospel in its tenderest form—Christ does not wait for sinners to make themselves fit but bids them come as they are, laden and weary, that He may give what they could never earn. The condition is simply to come; the rest is His own gift, double rest, a rest given and a rest found, peace with God and peace within.
webster_summary: Christ's tender invitation to the weary and sin-burdened to come to Him and receive rest as a free gift.
webster_full: COME UNTO ME, phrase (gospel invitation). From Matthew 11:28-30; the personal summons of Christ to laboring and heavy-laden sinners.
A free and universal call to all who are burdened with sin and weary of self-effort.
The offer of rest, given by Christ and found in His easy yoke and light burden.

As recorded in Scripture: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls” (Matthew 11:28-29).
By extension, the heart of evangelical preaching, which sets Christ forth as freely receiving the coming sinner.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the invitation is blunted wherever it is severed from repentance and the bearing of Christ's yoke.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The words are too plain and too precious to be twisted into ideology; the only real corruption is a soft and partial preaching that takes “Come unto me” and drops “Take my yoke upon you.” A gospel of rest without the yoke of discipleship is not the gospel Christ preached, for the same breath that promises rest commands submission to a meek and lowly Lord.

The principle to recover is the wholeness of the call. The free offer is genuinely free—Christ casts out none who come—yet coming means coming to a Master, taking His yoke and learning of Him. The rest He gives is found precisely in that yoke. To preach the invitation aright is to hold out both the gift and the yoke together, neither hardening the offer with conditions of merit nor softening it into license.
roots_summary: The invitation joins the imagery of burden, yoke, and rest into a single tender summons from Christ.
roots_lines: “Labour and are heavy laden” pictures souls toiling under sin and the law's demands.
“I will give you rest” sets the rest as Christ's gift, not man's achievement.
“Take my yoke upon you” calls the coming sinner to discipleship under a meek Lord.
“Ye shall find rest unto your souls” promises an inward peace beyond the gift of pardon.
John 6:37 secures the offer: him that cometh Christ will in no wise cast out.
usage: The phrase is the classic text for the free offer of the gospel to weary sinners.
Pastors press it upon the doubting and the heavy-hearted as Christ's own personal welcome.
Believers return to it in seasons of burden, hearing again the Master's call to rest.

etymology: From 2 Corinthians 4:17, “our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory”; the Greek baros (weight, heaviness) set against the lightness of present trial.
biblical_def: The eternal weight of glory is the surpassing, everlasting blessedness that God works for His people through their present afflictions. The Apostle sets the two in a holy contrast: the affliction is “light” and “but for a moment,” while the glory is “a far more exceeding and eternal weight.” The very heaviness of suffering is light when laid in the scale against a glory that has substance, mass, and abiding permanence. There is a divine arithmetic here that the eye of faith alone can reckon: the affliction does not merely precede the glory but worketh it, as the file polishes the gold and the furnace refines the silver. Therefore the saint is bidden to look “not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.” This is no stoic resignation but the gaze of faith fixed upon the unseen and abiding. The momentary lightness of trouble is swallowed up in the ponderous, enduring glory that Christ has purchased and stored up for His own. Let the believer, then, not faint under present trial; the heaviest cross of this life is feather-light beside the weight of glory laid up in heaven, and that glory is the more exceeding because it shall never end.
webster_summary: The surpassing and everlasting glory God works for His people through their light and momentary afflictions.
webster_full: ETERNAL WEIGHT OF GLORY, phrase (biblical expression). From 2 Corinthians 4:17; the Greek baros, weight or heaviness, set against momentary affliction.
The abiding and substantial blessedness of the saints in heaven, contrasted with the lightness of earthly trial.
A glory wrought out by affliction as the furnace refines and the file polishes.
As recorded in Scripture: “For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).
By extension, the believer's ground for patience and hope amid present suffering.
scriptures: For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though its comfort is lost wherever the eternal and unseen are exchanged for a gospel of present ease.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase is not the object of ideological attack, but it is quietly emptied by every teaching that promises the saints their best life now and shrinks heaven to a vague afterthought. A prosperity scheme that treats affliction as a sign of defective faith stands opposed to the Apostle, who makes affliction the very instrument that worketh glory.

The principle to recover is the divine proportion between affliction and glory. The believer is to weigh trial in the balance of eternity, where the heaviest sorrow is light and the unseen glory is exceeding and abiding. To fix the eye on the temporal is to faint; to fix it on the eternal is to endure. The cross of this present moment is the appointed road to the weight of glory, and the saint who looks past the seen to the unseen will not lose heart.
roots_summary: The phrase rests on a deliberate antithesis of light and weight, moment and eternity, seen and unseen.
roots_lines: “Light affliction” weighs the trial as small in the scale of faith.
“But for a moment” sets the brevity of suffering against the permanence of glory.
“Worketh for us” makes affliction the very instrument that produces the glory.
“Far more exceeding and eternal weight” piles up superlatives to magnify the glory's mass.
Verse 18 grounds the whole in looking at the unseen and eternal rather than the seen and temporal.
usage: The phrase consoles suffering believers by setting present trial against everlasting glory.
Preachers use it to teach the divine purpose of affliction in working out the saints' glory.
It guards the church against any gospel that promises ease in place of the cross.

etymology: From Philippians 3:20, “For our conversation is in heaven”; the Greek politeuma denotes commonwealth, citizenship, or seat of government—the believer's true country lying in heaven.
biblical_def: Heavenly citizenship is the truth that the believer's true commonwealth, home, and allegiance lie not on earth but in heaven, whence he looks for the Saviour. The word the Apostle uses, rendered “conversation” in the Authorized Version, signifies a citizenship or commonwealth; the saint is enrolled as a citizen of a heavenly country and lives on earth as a pilgrim and stranger. His politics, his loyalties, and his hopes are governed from above. This pilgrim character runs through all Scripture: Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God”; the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.” The believer, set down for a season in this world, holds it loosely, knowing he has here no continuing city but seeks one to come. His citizenship shapes his conduct: he walks worthy of the heavenly calling, sets his affection on things above, and refuses to be conformed to the present age. And his citizenship fixes his hope, for “from thence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body.” The pilgrim's journey ends not in dissolution but in resurrection glory, when the King shall come to bring His scattered citizens home to the city whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: The believer's true commonwealth and home in heaven, which governs his conduct and fixes his hope while he sojourns on earth.
webster_full: HEAVENLY CITIZENSHIP, phrase (biblical expression). From Philippians 3:20; the Greek politeuma, commonwealth or citizenship.
The believer's enrollment as a citizen of the heavenly country, with allegiance and hope fixed above.
The pilgrim character of the Christian, who sojourns on earth as a stranger seeking a city to come.
As recorded in Scripture: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).
By extension, the governing motive for holy conduct and the ground of the saint's hope of resurrection.
scriptures: Phi 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Col 3:1
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though its pilgrim hope is dulled wherever the church sinks its affections wholly into this present world.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase is not the prize of any ideological campaign, yet the truth it carries is steadily eroded by a worldliness that treats earth as the believer's home and heaven as a distant rumor. When the church loses the sense of pilgrimage, it grasps after earthly security and forgets the city which hath foundations.

The principle to recover is the pilgrim's posture. Heavenly citizenship is no excuse for idleness or for despising the duties of earthly life, for the saint serves faithfully in his calling; but it forbids him to set his heart below. He holds the world loosely, sets his affection on things above, and waits for the Saviour from heaven. So living, he walks worthy of the heavenly calling and is ready for the day when Christ shall fashion his lowly body like unto His glorious body.
roots_summary: The phrase draws on the language of commonwealth and pilgrimage that runs from the patriarchs to the Apostle.
roots_lines: Politeuma means a commonwealth or seat of citizenship, the believer's true country.
Philippians 3:20 names heaven as that commonwealth and Christ as the awaited Saviour.
Hebrews 11 paints the patriarchs as strangers and pilgrims seeking a heavenly city.
Colossians 3 commands the risen believer to seek the things that are above.
First Peter 2:11 binds the pilgrim identity to abstinence from fleshly lusts.
usage: The phrase teaches believers to hold earthly things loosely as pilgrims bound for heaven.
Preachers use it to fix the church's hope on the return of Christ from heaven.
It motivates holy conduct, for the citizen of heaven walks worthy of his calling on earth.

etymology: From Isaiah 42:3, “A bruised reed shall he not break,” quoted of Christ in Matthew 12:20; immortalized in Richard Sibbes' treatise The Bruised Reed and Smoking Flax (1630).
biblical_def: The bruised reed is the figure of a weak, broken, and contrite soul whom Christ will not cast off but tenderly restore. Isaiah prophesied of the Servant of the LORD, “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench,” and Matthew sets this gentleness at the very heart of Christ's ministry. A reed is a frail thing, and a bruised reed frailer still—fit, one would think, only to be trodden down; the smoking flax is a wick that no longer flames but only smolders, fit only to be put out. Yet the Lord deals not so. He will not break the one nor quench the other, but cherishes the least spark of grace and the feeblest sigh of penitence. Richard Sibbes, that sweet dropper of the Puritan age, drew from this text a whole physic for wounded consciences: that Christ came not to break but to bind up, not to quench but to fan into flame. The bruised reed is the sinner broken under conviction, the saint cast down by temptation, the doubting heart that fears it is too far gone. To all such Christ stoops in mercy. He bruises that He may heal, and where He has begun to bruise He will not break; He will bring forth judgment unto victory, perfecting the work He has begun until the smoking flax burns clear and the bruised reed stands upright in glory.
webster_summary: The figure of a weak and contrite soul whom Christ, far from breaking, tenderly binds up and restores.
webster_full: BRUISED REED, phrase (biblical expression). From Isaiah 42:3 and Matthew 12:20; made famous by Richard Sibbes' treatise The Bruised Reed (1630).
A frail and broken thing, here a symbol of the weak, wounded, and contrite believer.
The smoking flax, its companion figure, denotes the least spark of grace which Christ will not extinguish.
As recorded in Scripture: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Matthew 12:20).
By extension, the tenderness of Christ toward the feeble and the doubting members of His flock.
scriptures: Isa 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though Christ's tenderness is counterfeited wherever therapeutic affirmation is preached in place of healing grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The bruised reed is not seized by ideology, but its sweetness is easily corrupted into a sentimental gospel that affirms the sinner in his sin rather than binding up the contrite. Christ's gentleness to the bruised is not a refusal to deal with sin; He bruises before He heals, and the reed He spares is the one already broken under conviction.

The principle to recover is the discriminating tenderness of Christ. He will not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax—but the comfort is for the contrite, not the careless. Sibbes is careful here: Christ cherishes the least true grace and pours not vinegar but oil into the wound, yet He will at length bring forth judgment unto victory, perfecting His people. True comfort lifts up the cast-down saint without flattering the impenitent.
roots_summary: The phrase joins the prophetic figure of Isaiah with its Gospel fulfillment and its Puritan exposition.
roots_lines: Isaiah 42:3 sets the figure within the song of the LORD's gentle Servant.
Matthew 12:20 applies it to Christ amid His healing ministry and the rage of His enemies.
A “reed” is a frail marsh plant; “bruised” renders it weaker still.
“Smoking flax” is a smoldering wick, the faintest remaining spark of fire.
Richard Sibbes drew from the text a healing physic for wounded consciences.
usage: The phrase comforts weak and doubting believers with the tenderness of Christ.
Pastors apply it to souls broken under conviction or cast down by temptation.
It guards the gospel from harshness toward the contrite while still naming sin.

etymology: From Jeremiah 2:13, where Israel commits two evils: forsaking “the fountain of living waters” and hewing out “cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water”; a cistern being a hewn reservoir for stored rainwater.
biblical_def: Broken cisterns are the LORD's figure for every idol and false confidence men dig for themselves when they forsake Him. Through Jeremiah He charges His people with two evils: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.” The folly is double and exquisite. A fountain of living waters springs up fresh and inexhaustible without man's labor; a cistern is at best a stagnant pool of stored rain, and a broken cistern holds nothing at all. To leave the one for the other is the very madness of idolatry: to abandon an ever-flowing, freely-given spring and to toil with chisel and sweat to carve out a leaking pit that mocks the thirst it promises to slake. Every idol is such a cistern—wealth, pleasure, the praise of men, false religion, the broken comforts of the world. They cost much in the hewing and yield nothing in the drinking; the soul that trusts them dies of thirst beside its own cracked stonework. Here is the anatomy of every backsliding heart and every unconverted pursuit. The remedy is to return to the fountain, to forsake the broken cisterns and drink of the living waters that the LORD freely gives in Christ. He who is the spring of all satisfaction asks only that we leave the dry pits and come to Him who alone can quench the soul.
webster_summary: The LORD's figure for idols and false confidences—leaking reservoirs that men hew out when they forsake the fountain of living waters.
webster_full: BROKEN CISTERNS, phrase (biblical expression). From Jeremiah 2:13; a cistern being a hewn reservoir for stored rainwater, here cracked and unable to hold any.
A figure for every idol and false trust which costs labor in the making yet yields no satisfaction.
Set in contrast to the fountain of living waters, the freely flowing spring which is God Himself.

As recorded in Scripture: “For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13).
By extension, the folly of seeking the soul's rest in any creature apart from the Creator.
scriptures: Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Jer 2:11
Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.
Jon 2:8
They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy.
Psa 16:4
Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god: their drink offerings of blood will I not offer, nor take up their names into my lips.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the diagnosis is muted wherever idolatry is renamed self-fulfillment and the broken cistern is praised as a path to the self.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase is not a target of organized revision, yet the age has dignified the very cistern-hewing Jeremiah condemned: the relentless pursuit of self through wealth, pleasure, and personal expression is sold as the road to fulfillment. What Scripture calls a broken cistern the world calls a dream worth chasing.

The principle to recover is the folly of forsaking the fountain. Every idol is a cistern that costs much labor and holds no water; the soul cannot be filled by what it carves for itself. The remedy is not a better cistern but a return to the spring. To abandon the living waters for cracked stone is, the LORD says, an astonishing thing—let the heavens be astonished. The cure of idolatry is to come back to God in Christ, the fountain that never fails.
roots_summary: The phrase rests on the contrast between a living fountain and a hand-hewn, leaking reservoir.
roots_lines: A “cistern” is a hewn pit for storing rainwater, dependent and stagnant at best.
“Broken” renders it useless, cracked so it cannot hold even stored water.
Jeremiah 2:13 names two evils: forsaking the fountain and hewing the cistern.
The fountain of living waters is the LORD Himself, fresh and freely flowing.
The figure exposes every idol as costly to make and empty to drink.
usage: Preachers use broken cisterns to expose the emptiness of idols and worldly trusts.
The phrase diagnoses backsliding as forsaking the fountain for self-hewn pits.
Believers examine their hearts for cisterns hewn in place of drinking from God.

etymology: From Jeremiah 2:13, where the LORD names Himself “the fountain of living waters”; fulfilled in Christ's words at the well (John 4:10-14) and the feast (John 7:37-39). “Living waters” means fresh, running, spring water.
biblical_def: The fountain of living waters is a title of the LORD Himself, and of Christ who freely gives the Spirit—the soul's one true and inexhaustible satisfaction. In Jeremiah the LORD mourns that His people have forsaken Him, “the fountain of living waters,” for broken cisterns. A fountain of living waters is no stagnant pool but a spring of fresh, running water, ever flowing, never failing, freely available to all who come. Such is God to His people. The figure flowers fully in the Gospel of John. To the woman at the well Christ says, “If thou knewest the gift of God… thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water,” and again, “the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.” At the feast He cries, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink”—and John explains, “this spake he of the Spirit.” Here is the whole gospel in a figure: the thirsty soul, parched and weary of broken cisterns, is bidden to come to Christ and drink. The water He gives is the Spirit, who springs up within unto everlasting life. The fountain costs the comer nothing, for Christ has paid all; it never runs dry, for it is God Himself; and it alone can satisfy, for the soul was made for Him.
webster_summary: A title of the LORD, and of Christ who gives the Spirit—the fresh, freely flowing spring that alone satisfies the thirsty soul.
webster_full: FOUNTAIN OF LIVING WATERS, phrase (biblical title of God). From Jeremiah 2:13; “living waters” meaning fresh, running spring water, here a title of God Himself.
The inexhaustible spring of all satisfaction, contrasted with the broken cisterns of idols.
Fulfilled in Christ, who gives living water that springs up into everlasting life.
As recorded in Scripture: “Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God… thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water” (John 4:10).
By extension, the gift of the Holy Spirit, freely poured out on all who come to Christ and drink.
scriptures: Jer 2:13
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
Joh 4:14
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
Joh 7:37
In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the soul's thirst is misdirected wherever the world is offered as the satisfaction only God can give.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The figure is not the object of ideological dispute, but the truth it carries cuts against the whole spirit of an age that bids the thirsty soul drink at every cistern but the true Fountain. Wealth, pleasure, and the endless pursuit of self are pressed as the springs of satisfaction, when they are the very broken cisterns Jeremiah named.

The principle to recover is that God alone satisfies. The soul was made for Him and thirsts until it drinks of Him; no creature can fill the cistern He alone was made to fill. The remedy is the free offer of the gospel: “let him that is athirst come… and take the water of life freely.” Christ stands at the feast still crying, “If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.” The fountain is open, full, and free; the only condition is to come thirsty.
roots_summary: The figure runs from Jeremiah's title of God to Christ's gift of the Spirit and the open invitation of Revelation.
roots_lines: “Living waters” means fresh, running spring water as opposed to stored or stagnant.
Jeremiah 2:13 names the LORD Himself as that fountain, forsaken for broken cisterns.
John 4 has Christ offering living water that springs up into everlasting life.
John 7:37-39 identifies the living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Revelation 22:17 issues the final invitation to take the water of life freely.
usage: The phrase names God and Christ as the soul's only true and lasting satisfaction.
Preachers set the fountain against broken cisterns to press the free offer of the gospel.
Believers return to it when parched, drinking afresh of Christ and His Spirit.

etymology: From 1 Peter 5:7, “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you”; echoing Psalm 55:22, “Cast thy burden upon the LORD.” To “cast” is to throw off or commit wholly.
biblical_def: Casting cares is the believer's duty and remedy against anxiety—the act of throwing the whole weight of his burdens upon God, who lovingly bears them for him. Peter binds the command to humility: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God… casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.” The casting is total: not some cares but all, not a partial unburdening but a full committal of every anxious weight into the hands of the Almighty. And it rests on a tender ground—“for he careth for you.” The God upon whom we cast our cares is not indifferent; He is mindful, watchful, and fatherly toward His own. The Psalmist had sung the same long before: “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.” Here is the divine cure for the corroding sin of worry. Anxiety is at root a failure to trust the providence and the love of God; it stoops the soul under a load God never meant it to carry alone. To cast care is an act of humble faith—it confesses that we are not sovereign and that He is, that we cannot sustain ourselves and that He can. The Apostle Paul prescribes the same medicine: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.” The fruit is peace that passeth understanding, the quiet of a soul that has rolled its burden onto the One who never sleeps.
webster_summary: The believer's duty to throw all anxious burdens upon God, who in fatherly love cares for and sustains His people.
webster_full: CASTING CARES, phrase (biblical exhortation). From 1 Peter 5:7, echoing Psalm 55:22; to “cast” meaning to throw off or commit wholly.
The act of committing every anxious burden into the hands of God.
Grounded in the assurance that God cares for and sustains those who trust Him.
As recorded in Scripture: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1 Peter 5:7).
By extension, the divine remedy against the sin of worry and the medicine of believing prayer.
scriptures: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
Phi 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the duty is hollowed wherever anxiety is treated only as a feeling to be managed rather than a burden to be cast on God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The exhortation is not the prize of any ideological campaign, yet the age offers a counterfeit cure. Where Scripture commands the believer to cast his care upon a personal, providing God, the spirit of the times reduces anxiety to a self-managed mood and bids the troubled soul look inward for peace rather than upward to its Maker.

The principle to recover is that worry is cured by committal, not by introspection. To cast care is an act of humble faith in the sovereignty and fatherly love of God; it confesses that He is on the throne and we are not. The believer does not deny real burdens but rolls them, with believing prayer and thanksgiving, onto the One who careth for him. The fruit is the peace of God that passeth understanding—a quiet born not of self-soothing but of resting in providence.
roots_summary: The phrase joins the Psalmist's ancient counsel with the Apostle's charge and the cure of believing prayer.
roots_lines: To “cast” is to throw off entirely, committing the whole weight elsewhere.
Psalm 55:22 sets the pattern: cast the burden on the LORD and be sustained.
First Peter 5:7 binds the casting to humility under God's mighty hand.
“For he careth for you” grounds the duty in God's fatherly love.
Philippians 4:6 prescribes prayer with thanksgiving as the means of casting.
usage: The phrase counsels anxious believers to commit every burden into God's hands.
Pastors press it as the divine cure for the corroding sin of worry.
It directs the troubled soul to believing prayer rather than self-reliance.

etymology: From the Old English druncen, the state of intoxication; treated in Scripture as a work of the flesh and a sin against sobriety, notably Ephesians 5:18, Proverbs 23:29-35, and 1 Corinthians 6:10.
biblical_def: Drunkenness is the sin of intoxication, condemned throughout Scripture as a work of the flesh that wars against the sobriety and self-government of the Spirit-filled life. The Apostle sets the contrast sharply: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.” The same man cannot be ruled by wine and ruled by the Spirit; the one is excess and dissipation, the other is order, watchfulness, and praise. Proverbs paints the drunkard's misery with unflinching realism—woe, sorrow, contentions, wounds without cause, redness of eyes; the cup that “at the last… biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder”; the captive who, beaten and sick, can only ask, “I will seek it yet again.” That is the bondage of the sin: it promises mirth and delivers slavery. Paul lists drunkards among those who “shall not inherit the kingdom of God,” setting the sin in dreadful company. Scripture does not forbid wine as such—it is called a gift that gladdens the heart of man—but it forbids the surrender of reason and self-control to drink. The Christian is called to sobriety because he is a watchman, a soldier, a son of light who must not sleep as do others. The Spirit-filled life is a sober life: vigilant in prayer, governed in appetite, ready for the Master's return. The remedy for the drunkard is not mere temperance but new birth—to be filled with the Spirit, whose fruit is the temperance that drink could never give.
webster_summary: The sin of intoxication, condemned in Scripture as a work of the flesh opposed to sobriety and to the Spirit-filled life.
webster_full: DRUNKENNESS, phrase (doctrinal/ethical topic). From Old English druncen; in Scripture a work of the flesh, condemned in Ephesians 5:18 and 1 Corinthians 6:10.
The state of intoxication wherein reason and self-government are surrendered to drink.
Set in direct contrast to being filled with the Spirit, which produces sobriety and temperance.
As recorded in Scripture: “And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).
By extension, a bondage that promises mirth yet delivers misery, woe, and the loss of God's kingdom to the impenitent.
scriptures: Eph 5:18
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath babbling? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes?
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
Gal 5:21
Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like: of the which I tell you before, as I have also told you in time past, that they which do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: The live corruption is the modern normalization and even celebration of drunkenness as harmless fun, recreation, or a personal right.
corruption_paragraphs: The present age has not so much redefined drunkenness as rebranded it. What Scripture names a work of the flesh that bars from the kingdom, the culture treats as harmless recreation, a deserved release, even a mark of conviviality and good cheer. Intoxication is celebrated in advertising and entertainment, excused as a way to unwind, and pressed upon the young as a rite of belonging. The drunkard of Proverbs—beaten, sick, and crying “I will seek it yet again”—is recast as the life of the party. To call it sin is treated as joyless and intolerant; to call it bondage is dismissed as old-fashioned. Yet the serpent in the cup bites no less today than in Solomon's time.

The principle to recover is sobriety as a Christian calling, not a killjoy rule. Scripture does not despise wine, which gladdens the heart, but it forbids the surrender of reason to it; the believer is a watchman and a soldier who must keep his head clear for prayer and readiness. Against the celebration of excess stands the apostolic command: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit. The cure is not mere abstinence by willpower but the new birth and the Spirit's fruit of temperance, which alone can free the captive of the cup.
roots_summary: The doctrine rests on the apostolic contrast between drunken excess and Spirit-filled sobriety.
roots_lines: Druncen, the Old English root, names the state of intoxication itself.
Ephesians 5:18 sets drunkenness against being filled with the Spirit.
Proverbs 23:29-35 paints the drunkard's misery and his serpentine bondage.
First Corinthians 6:10 and Galatians 5:21 bar drunkards from the kingdom.
Sobriety is commanded of the watchful son of light who awaits his Lord.
usage: Preachers cite the sin of drunkenness to call sinners to sobriety and the Spirit-filled life.
The doctrine confronts the modern celebration of intoxication as harmless recreation.
Believers are exhorted to temperance as watchmen ready for the Master's return.
